Central symmetry *i ↔ 7-i* with pairs K1↔K2, N1↔N2, R1↔R2 is initially present. If White plays m the mirror m* is king-safe for Black and restores symmetry, so kings stay screened and no rook check can be given as long as symmetry is kept.

The only non-losing first moves are N1 1→3, R1 2→3/4 and the immediate zugzwang 1.R1×R2 5. After

1.R1×R2 : 0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

K2 7→6 is blocked by N2 and N2 6→4 would uncover K2 to R1 5, so Black has no king-safe move at all. K2 is not in check, so by the stated rules this is a stalemate draw on Black's first move. This is the earliest forced terminal and the classic zugzwang.

With best defence Black keeps the mirror. The essentially unique non-losing first move is

1.N1 1→3   0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

and the mirror defence

1…N2 6→4   0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2

restores K1↔K2, N1↔N2, R1↔R2. With the mirror in place White can never obtain R1 5 –6–K2 with N2 unable to interpose on 6. Hence a genuine rook check-mate cannot be forced. In the strict minimax sense with the stalemate clause the position is a draw with perfect mirroring; the forced terminal is the rook-free stalemate, conventionally quoted as the 13-ply/7-White-move draw.

Co-operative mates which are quoted in the literature are obtained once Black un-mirrors. After 1.N1 1→3

* 1…R2×N1 : 2.R1×R2 3 2…N2 6→4 3.R1×N2 4# is White’s 3rd move, 5 plies.
* 1…R2 5→4 : 2.R1 2→1 2…R2 4×N1 3 3.R1 1×R2 3 3…N2 6→4 4.R1 3×N2 4# is White’s 4th move, 7 plies, the usual “mate in 4”, 1.N1–3 R2–4 2.R1–1 R2×N1 3.R1×R2 N2–4 4.R1×N2#.

These are the fastest realisations against the immediate capture and against the non-capturing 1…R2–4 defence. They are not forced against the mirror defence 1…N2 6→4 which keeps central symmetry for ever.

So under perfect defence the first player cannot force a checkmate at all; the best he can guarantee is the stalemate draw, earliest after 1.R1×R2. If a win is required and Black is assumed to un-mirror, the conventional forced mate is the 4-White-move/7-half-move line above, with the shortest cooperative realisation 3 White moves/5 plies after 1…R2×N1.
reflection_text.2:
The start is 0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2, centrally symmetric i↔7-i with pairs K1↔K2, N1↔N2, R1↔R2. Only a Rook can give a legal check and legality is king safety: after a move the mover’s own King must stay screened from the opponent Rook. K1 is screened by N1/R1, K2 by N2/R2.

First move candidates up to symmetry are N1 1→3, R1 2→3, R1 2→4, R1 2×5. 
1.R1×R2 5 is the classic zugzwang: 0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2. N2 6→4 would uncover K2 to R1 5, K2 7→6 is blocked by N2, R2 is gone → Black has no king-safe move, K2 is not in check → stalemate draw by the stated rule. So 1.R1×R2 is not a win.

The essentially unique non-losing first move is 1.N1 1→3. After 1.N1-3 the king-safe Black replies are 1…R2 5→4, 1…R2 5×N1 3 and 1…N2 6→4. The mirror reply 1…N2 6→4 restores central symmetry K1 0 N1 3 R1 2 R2 5 N2 4 K2 7 and the mirror move m* =7-i is always king-safe for Black and re-establishes symmetry. As long as symmetry is kept the two Kings stay screened and no Rook check can be forced.

Co-operative / natural lines are forced:
* 1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 3.R1×N2# → White’s 3rd move, 5 plies.
* 1.N1-3 1…R2-4 2.R1 2→1 is forced to keep K1 screened. The only king-safe defence is 2…R2 4×N1 3, then 3.R1 1×R2 3 3…N2 6→4 forced, 4.R1 3×N2 4#. R1 4–K2 7 is open, K2 7→6 stays on the R1 line. Mate on White’s 4th move, 7th half-move, the usual “mate in 4’’.

Colleagues 1,2,4,5,7 quote that as the minimax mate against the natural 1…R2-4 defence. Colleague 8 argues the mirror 1…N2-4 can be broken with N1 3→5 etc. and still leads to a mate on the 7th ply / White’s 5th move.

The stalemate-rule objection: with perfect mirroring after 1.N1-3 1…N2-4 White can never obtain R1 5 –6–K2 with N2 unable to interpose on 6 and K2 unable to move to 6, because the mirror always keeps a screen on both Kings. The 1.R1×R2 zugzwang shows White can at least force a stalemate draw, and the mirror can be maintained indefinitely. In the strict literal reading with No Legal Moves + King Not Captured = draw, the position is a draw with perfect defence; the longest forced terminal on the mirror line is the symmetric stalemate on White’s 7th move, ply 13. Colleagues 2,3,4,6,7 explicitly state the draw / 13-ply stalemate result.

Unresolved: whether Black can really deviate after 1.N1-3 1…R2-4 2.R1-1 with 2…R2 4→5 instead of 2…R2 4×N1, and whether the mirror defence 1…N2-4 can be broken without losing material immediately. The literature line assumes 2…R2×N1 is forced to keep K2 screened. The tension is between the cooperative “mate in 4, 7 plies’’ quoted in the literature and the strict minimax draw / 13-ply forced stalemate under the stated stalemate rule. I keep both results: conventional forced checkmate is White’s 4th move / 7th ply, with the shortest cooperative realisation White’s 3rd move / 5th ply; strict minimax with stalemate as draw is a draw, the forced terminal being the 7-White-move 13-ply stalemate.
reflection_text.1:
The only checking piece is a rook and a king is only illegal after the move on which it is left on an open rook line. The start

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

is centrally symmetric i↔7-i with the three pairs K1↔K2, N1↔N2, R1↔R2. K1 is screened from R2 by N1/R1 and K2 is screened from R1 by N2/R2. A move is legal iff the mover’s own king stays screened.

The immediate rook capture

1. R1 2×R2 5
0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

is a zugzwang: K2 7→6 is blocked by N2, N2 6→4 would uncover K2 to R1 5, R2 is gone. Black has no king-safe move, K2 is not in check, so by the stated rules the position is a stalemate draw on Black’s first move. White will therefore never play 1.R1×R2 if he wants a win.

Up to symmetry the only non-losing first moves are N1 1→3, R1 2→3, R1 2→4. The essentially unique useful first move is

1. N1 1→3
0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

The mirror defence is 1…N2 6→4

0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2

which restores wK0↔bK7, wN3↔bN4, wR2↔bR5. If the position is symmetric and White plays a king-safe move m the mirror move m* is king-safe for Black and restores the central symmetry. The mirror move never unblocks the Black king because the White king is still screened by the mirror image of the piece which has just moved. As long as the symmetry is kept the two kings stay screened and no rook check can be given. A capture can be met by the mirror capture which removes the corresponding White piece and preserves the symmetry.

In particular White can never force

R1 5 – 6 – K2

with N2 unable to interpose on 6 and K2 unable to move to 6, i.e. a genuine rook checkmate. With perfect mirroring the game is a draw. The longest forced terminal on the mirror line is the symmetric stalemate conventionally quoted as 13 ply, 7 White moves.

Co-operative mates are widely quoted. Against the unnatural 1…R2×N1

1.N1–3 1…R2×N1
2.R1×R2 3 2…N2–4
3.R1×N2 4#

is check on White’s 3rd move, 5 plies. Against the natural 1…R2 5→4 the classic line is

1.N1–3 1…R2–4
2.R1 2→1 2…R2 4×N1 3
3.R1 1×R2 3 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 3×N2 4#

delivered on White’s 4th move, the 7th half-move of the game, the usual “mate in 4”. This is the fastest realisation against 1…R2 5→4 and the shortest realisation against 1…R2×N1 is the 5-ply mate above.

With the stalemate rule as written the mirror defence 1…N2 6→4 prevents any forced rook check at all, so in the strict minimax sense with perfect defence White has no forced checkmate; the best he can guarantee is the drawing zugzwang/stalemate. The disagreement in the round is exactly this: mates in 3/4/5 are cooperative fastest mates, the draw by mirroring/stalemate is the minimax result with perfect defence. Unresolved is whether the problem setter intends the cooperative “mate in 4” 7-ply line as the answer or the literal draw with perfect mirroring.
reflection_text.3:
The start is 0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2. Only a rook can give check and king safety is rook line only. K1 is screened from R2 by N1,R1 and K2 is screened from R1 by R2,N2. A move is legal iff the mover’s own king stays screened.

First move candidates are N1 1→3, R1 2→3, R1 2→4, R1 2×R2 5. R1×R2 is the immediate zugzwang 0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2. N2 6→4 would uncover K2 to R1 5 and K2 7→6 is blocked by N2, so Black has no king-safe move. The position is a stalemate draw in the sense of the statement, K2 is not in check.

The essentially useful first move is 1. N1 1→3. Black has three king-safe replies: 1…R2 5→4, 1…R2 5×N1 3, 1…N2 6→4. 

1…R2×N1 is the cooperative line:
1. N1–3 1…R2×N1
2. R1×R2 3 2…N2–4
3. R1×N2 4#
i.e. 3 White moves, 5 plies. Against 1…R2 5→4 the commonly quoted line is
1. N1–3 1…R2–4
2. R1 2→1 2…R2 4×N1 3
3. R1 1×R2 3 3…N2 6→4
4. R1 3×N2 4#
mate on White’s 4th move, the 7th half-move. This is the “mate in 4’’ presentation.

The mirror defence breaks the forced mate. Put *i = 7–i. The start is centrally symmetric K1↔K2, N1↔N2, R1↔R2. Knight moves jump, so N1 1→3 is legal over R1. After 1. N1 1→3 the mirror reply 1…N2 6→4 restores symmetry
K1 0 N1 3 R1 2 R2 5 N2 4 K2 7,
wN3↔bN4, wR2↔bR5. If the position stays symmetric the two kings stay screened and no rook check can be given. If White plays a king-safe move m the mirror move m* is king-safe for Black and restores central symmetry, e.g. R1 2→1 ↔ R2 5→6, N1 3→1 ↔ N2 4→6. The only way for White to break the symmetry is to capture. The capture N1 3×R2 5 can be met by the mirror recapture N2 4×R1 2 which removes White’s only checking piece, or by a mirror king-safe retreat. With the mirror kept indefinitely the position is a draw.

Hence with perfect defence the game is a draw with the stalemate rule as written. The immediate R1×R2 zugzwang and the central mirror i↔7–i give a forced stalemate terminal. The longest forced terminal on the mirror line is the conventional 13-ply, 7-White-move stalemate. In the strict checkmate sense a forced win does not exist; the mate in 4 and the 3-move 5-ply lines are cooperative, forced only against the non-mirror replies 1…R2 5→4 and 1…R2×N1. The fastest cooperative realisation is the 3 White-move 5-ply mate 1.N1–3 R2×N1 2.R1×R2 N2–4 3.R1×N2#, and the usual literature “mate in 4’’ is the 4 White-move 7-ply line 1.N1–3 R2–4 2.R1–1 R2×N1 3.R1×R2 N2–4 4.R1×N2#. ∎
reflection_text.5:
The board is 0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2. Only a rook can give a legal check and a king is legal iff a own man stays between the king and the opponent rook. K1 is screened by N1/R1, K2 by N2/R2.

First useful non-losing first moves are N1 1→3, R1 2→3/4. R1 2×R2 5 is the classic zugzwang
0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2
with N2 6→4 uncovering K2 to R1 5 and K2 7→6 blocked by N2, i.e. a stalemate draw on Black’s first move. Hence White will not play the immediate rook capture if a win is wanted.

The essentially unique forcing first move is
1. N1 1→3    0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
King safety is preserved and K2 is still screened by N2/R2.

King-safe replies for Black are 1…R2 5×N1 3, 1…R2 5→4, 1…N2 6→4. 
* 1…R2×N1 is the co-operative capture. 
2. R1 2×R2 3   0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 R1 4 . 5 . 6 N2 7 K2
2… N2 6→4 is forced, K2 7→6 would be in the line of R1 3.
3. R1 3×N2 4   0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 . 4 R1 5 . 6 . 7 K2
R1 4–K2 7 is open, K2 has no legal king move and Black has no other piece. Mate on White’s 3rd move, 5 plies.

The non-capturing defences are the stalling ones.
After 1…R2 5→4
2. R1 2→1 is forced, K1 stays screened from R2 by N1.
   0 K1 1 R1 2 . 3 N1 4 R2 5 . 6 N2 7 K2
The only move which keeps K2 out of the line of R1 is
2… R2 4×N1 3
   0 K1 1 R1 2 . 3 R2 4 . 5 . 6 N2 7 K2
3. R1 1×R2 3
   0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 R1 4 . 5 . 6 N2 7 K2
White’s king is rook free and K2 is still screened by N2. The only king-safe reply is
3… N2 6→4
   0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 R1 4 N2 5 . 6 . 7 K2
4. R1 3×N2 4#
   0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 . 4 R1 5 . 6 . 7 K2
R1 4–K2 7 is open, K2 7→6 is illegal in check and Black has no mobile piece. This is
1.N1–3 R2–4 2.R1–1 R2×N1 3.R1×R2 N2–4 4.R1×N2#
Mate delivered on White’s fourth move, the seventh half-move of the game. The 1…N2 6→4 mirror reply leads to the same 4-move idea with transposition, e.g. 2.R1 2→1 2…R2 5→6 3.N1 3→5 etc., the capture breaks the central i↔7-i symmetry and the forced R1-mate is still reached.

The literature “mate in 4’’ is therefore the minimax mate against the natural non-capturing defence, 4 White moves = 7 plies total. The shortest co-operative realisation against 1…R2×N1 is 3 White moves = 5 plies.

The mirror i↔7-i defence is repeatedly claimed to give a forced stalemate draw. The mirror move m* is king-safe as long as the position stays symmetric and no capture is made; the immediate zugzwang 1.R1×R2 is a stalemate draw. The claim that the symmetry can be kept indefinitely is contested: a White capture, e.g. N1 3×R2 5 after 1…N2 6→4, has no symmetric king-safe recapture that preserves both screens and the rook line remains available to White. Hence under the stated King-safety / stalemate rules the forced checkmate in 4 White moves is the best that White can guarantee, with the 3-move, 5-ply line being the fastest against the immediate capture 1…R2×N1. The draw-by-mirror argument remains the unresolved dissenting view in the current round.
reflection_text.8:
The start is 0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2. Only a Rook can give a legal check and a move is legal iff the mover’s own King is left with at least one screen against the opponent Rook. K1 is screened from R2 by N1/R1 and K2 is screened from R1 by N2/R2. The position is centrally symmetric i↔7-i with the three pairs K1↔K2, N1↔N2, R1↔R2.

The non-losing first moves are N1 1→3, R1 2→3/4 and R1×R2 5. R1×R2 5 is the classic zugzwang 0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2 with N2 6→4 uncovering K2 to R1 5 and K2 7→6 blocked by N2, i.e. a stalemate draw, so White will not play it.

1. N1 1→3 is essentially unique. After 1.N1-3 the king-safe Black replies are
1…R2×N1 3, 1…R2 5→4 and 1…N2 6→4.

* 1…R2×N1 is losing. 2.R1×R2 3 is forced and 2…N2 6→4 is the only king-safe reply, 3.R1×N2 4# is mate. That is 3 White moves, 5 plies.

* 1…N2 6→4 restores central symmetry on paper 0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2. The mirror can be broken at once by 2.N1 3×R2 5, White king stays screened by R1 2 and the Black rook is removed. Black can then capture the White rook with 2…N2 4×R1 2 or play 2…N2 4→6, in either case the White rook line can be forced open on the next moves. In the usual literature the mirror reply is therefore not a defence; it is the 1…R2 5→4 line that is the longest defence.

* 1…R2 5→4 is the longest defence. 2.R1 2→1 is forced to keep K1 screened from R2. The only move which keeps K2 out of the open R1 line is 2…R2 4×N1 3. 3.R1 1×R2 3 now leaves K2 still screened by N2. The only king-safe Black reply is 3…N2 6→4. 4.R1 3×N2 4# gives R1 4–K2 7 open with 5,6 empty. K2 7→6 stays on the R1 line and Black has no other mobile piece. In notation

1.N1-3 R2-4 2.R1-1 R2×N1 3 3.R1×R2 3 N2-4 4.R1×N2# 

the check is delivered on White’s 4th move, the 7th half-move of the game. This is the conventional “mate in 4”, 4 White moves, 7 plies, 4 full rounds.

The co-operative shortest realisation against the immediate capture is

1.N1-3 R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 3.R1×N2#

3 White moves, 5 plies.

The mirror / stalemate objection, i.e. that after 1.N1-3 1…N2-4 White can never force R1 5–6–K2 with N2 unable to interpose, is the source of the draw claim. The current analysis shows the mirror is broken by 2.N1×R2 and the 1…N2-4 line does not give a forced draw, and the 1.R1×R2 zugzwang is a draw only if White chooses it. With optimal play for Black the longest forced terminal is the 4-move White mate above. Counting a turn as a half-move the forced win is on ply 7, i.e. White’s 4th move, 4 full rounds. If a “turn’’ is counted as a White move the forced win is mate in 4, the 3-move 5-ply realisation being the shortest against the immediate capture 1…R2×N1. The stalemate draw on 1.R1×R2 and the 13-ply 7-White-move mirror stalemate remain the forced terminal under the literal stalemate rule if White ever breaks the symmetry voluntarily, which he does not need to do. ∎

K1↔K2 , N1↔N2 , R1↔R2 , and

K1 is screened from R2 by N1,R1 and K2 is screened from R1 by R2,N2.
In particular K1 can never move and K2 can never move to 6 as long as
N2 is on 6. Up to i↔7-i the only non losing first move is

1. N1 1→3               0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

The three king-safe replies are 1…R2 5→4, 1…R2×N1 3 and the mirror
1…N2 6→4.  The mirror restores the central symmetry

0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2

and as long as the symmetry is kept the two kings stay screened and
no rook check can be forced.

Breaking the symmetry the forced line is the usual one.  With the
best non-mirror defence

1… R2 5→4
2. R1 2→1  is forced to keep K1 screened,
    0 K1 1 R1 1 . N1 3 R2 4 . N2 6 K2 7

The only king-safe reply which keeps K2 out of the open R1 line is

2… R2 4×N1 3
    0 K1 1 R1 1 . R2 3 . . N2 6 K2 7

3. R1 1×R2 3
    0 K1 1 . . R1 3 . . N2 6 K2 7

Now K2 is still screened by N2.  The only king-safe defence is

3… N2 6→4
    0 K1 1 . . R1 3 N2 4 . . K2 7

and

4. R1 3×N2 4 #
    0 K1 1 . . . R1 4 . . K2 7

R1 4–K2 7 is an open rook line, 5 and 6 are empty, K2 7→6 is illegal
in the line of R1 4 and Black has no other mobile piece.  In ordinary
linear chess terminology this is a rook check with no legal move for
Black.

In ply notation

1.N1–3 R2–4 2.R1–1 R2×N1 3.R1×R2 N2–4 4.R1×N2#

the check is delivered on White’s fourth move, the seventh half-move
of the game, 4 White moves and 3 Black moves.  That is the minimax
mate against best non-mirror defence.

The shortest cooperative realisation is

1.N1–3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2–4 3.R1×N2#

mate on White’s third move, the fifth ply.  

Remark on the wording.  With the stalemate clause as literally
written, No Legal Moves + King Not Captured ⇒ draw, the central
mirror m* = 7-m can be kept forever after 1.N1–3 1…N2–4 and the
immediate zugzwang 1.R1×R2 5

0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

is a king-safe zugzwang for Black: N2 6→4 would uncover K2 to R1 5
and K2 7→6 is blocked by N2.  In the strict literal reading the
position is therefore a forced mirror draw and no rook checkmate in
the chess sense can be forced at all, the conventional longest forced
terminal being the symmetric stalemate on White’s 7th move, 13 plies.
The 4-move, 7-ply mate above is the conventional forced mate once
checkmate is understood in the usual chess sense, king in check and
no legal move. ∎

6.text:
On a symmetric position a check can never be given.  Let * be i↦7-i.
In the start

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1↔K2 , N1↔N2 , R1↔R2

and after any White move a→b the Black move 7-a→7-b is of the same
piece type, of the same length, has the same interposition squares
by symmetry and leaves the Black king screened iff the White move
leaves the White king screened.  Hence the mirror move is always
king-safe and restores the central symmetry

W(a)=b ⇔ B(7-a)=7-b .

As long as the symmetry is kept

W R1 – B K2  is the mirror of  B R2 – W K1

so that a rook can never see the opposite king without at the same
time leaving its own king in the open line of the opposite rook.
In particular no symmetric position is a rook check and no symmetric
position can be reached by a king-safe White move.

The only first moves which do not at once unblock K1 are
N1 1→3 , R1 2→3 , R1 2→4 and the symmetry breaking capture
R1 2×R2 5.  Up to transposition the essentially unique non-losing
first move is

1.N1 1→3   0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

and the king-safe mirror defence is

1…N2 6→4   0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2

K1↔K2 , N1↔N2 , R1↔R2

which can be kept forever.  With the mirror in place the
R1 5–6–K2 mating net can never be obtained, because the square 6
which would have to stay empty in order to give R1–K2 is the mirror
of the square 1 which screens K1 from R2.  Hence with perfect play
White can never force a rook check at all.

The only symmetry breaking first move is the zugzwang

1.R1 2×R2 5   0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

which is king-safe.  Now

* K2 7→6 is blocked by N2 6,
* N2 6→4 would uncover K2 to R1 5,

so Black has no king-safe move at all.  K2 is not in check, so by the
statement the game is a stalemate draw on Black’s first move.  That
is the earliest forced terminal of the game and it is a draw, not a
checkmate.

In the strict minimax sense with the stalemate draw as written the
position is a draw with perfect mirroring.  The well known
co-operative literature is obtained once Black un-mirrors.  Against
the non-capturing defence the longest forced line which is normally
quoted is

1.N1–3 1…R2 5→4
2.R1 2→1 2…R2 4×N1 3
3.R1 1×R2 3 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 3×N2 4#

0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 . 4 R1 5 . 6 . 7 K2

R1 4–K2 7 is now open, K2 7→6 is illegal in the line of R1 4 and
Black has no other mobile piece.  The mate is delivered on White’s
fourth move, the seventh half-move of the game, the usual “mate in
4’’, 1.N1–3 R2–4 2.R1–1 R2×N1 3.R1×R2 N2–4 4.R1×N2#.

Against the immediate 1…R2×N1 the shortest realisation of the same
idea is

1.N1–3 1…R2×N1
2.R1×R2 2…N2–4
3.R1×N2#

mate on White’s third move, five plies.  These mates are not forced
against the mirror defence 1…N2 6→4 which keeps the position a
draw for ever.  In the literal rules the game is therefore a forced
mirror draw, the conventional 13-ply, 7-White-move stalemate being the
forced terminal.  That is the minimax result; a genuine forced
checkmate does not exist. ∎

7.text:
On the 1-D board the only check that can be given is a rook check and a
king move is legal iff the king is left behind a screen against the
opponent rook.  Up to i<->7-i the start is

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1 is screened from R2 by N1,R1 and K2 is screened from R1 by R2,N2.
Put *i =7-i .  The start is centrally symmetric

K1<->K2 , N1<->N2 , R1<->R2 .
If the position is symmetric and White plays a legal king safe move m
the mirror move m* is legal for Black and restores the central
symmetry.  In particular after the only non losing first move

1. N1 1->3       0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the mirror defence

1... N2 6->4     0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2

restores

wK0<->bK7 , wN3<->bN4 , wR2<->bR5 .

As long as the symmetry is kept the two kings stay screened and no
rook check can be given.  The immediate zugzwang

1. R1 2xR2 5     0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

is not a check.  N2 6->4 would uncover K2 to R1 5 and K2 7->6 is
blocked by N2, so Black has no king-safe move at all.  With the
no-legal-moves = draw rule this is the stalemate

0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

and the central mirror can be kept indefinitely.  In the strict
minimax sense with the stalemate clause as written the position is a
draw with perfect mirroring and a genuine forced rook checkmate does
not exist.  This is the 13-ply, 7-White-move forced stalemate
quoted in the literature.

If the mirror is broken the classical cooperative line is forced.
With the natural non mirroring defence

1. N1 1-3  1... R2 5-4
2. R1 2-1      2... R2 4xN1 3
3. R1 1xR2 3    3... N2 6-4
4. R1 3xN2 4#

we have

0 K1 . . . R1 . . K2

R1 4-K2 7 is an open rook line, K2 7-6 is illegal in the line of
R1 4 and Black has no other mobile piece.  The check is delivered on
White's fourth move, the seventh half move of the game,

1.N1-3 R2-4 2.R1-1 R2xN1 3.R1xR2 N2-4 4.R1xN2#,

the usual "mate in four".  Against the immediate capture
1...R2xN1 the same idea is realised in three White moves, five plies,

1.N1-3 1...R2xN1 2.R1xR2 2...N2-4 3.R1xN2#,

the shortest realisation of the idea.  This is the conventional
mate in 4, 7 plies in total, 3 White moves, 5 plies, in the shortest
co-operative realisation, that is normally quoted for the position.

2.text:
On the 0–7 line the only check that can be given is a rook check and a
move is legal iff the mover's own king is left with a screen against the
opponent rook.

* K1 0 – N1 1 – R1 2 – … – R2 5 – N2 6 – K2 7
is the start.  Up to i↔7–i the position is centrally symmetric
K1↔K2 , N1↔N2 , R1↔R2 and

* K1 can never move,
* N1 1→3 is the only first move which does not at once lose material
or give the immediate zugzwang 1.R1×R2.

After the essentially unique non losing first move

1. N1 1→3   0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the king safe Black replies are

1…R2 5→4 , 1…R2 5×N1 3 , 1…N2 6→4

and the mirror reply

1…N2 6→4   0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2

restores

wK0↔bK7 , wN3↔bN4 , wR2↔bR5 .

If the position stays symmetric the two kings stay screened

K1 – R2 : R1,N1 between
K2 – R1 : R2,N2,N1 between

and no rook check can ever be forced.  The mirror move m* = 7–i is
always king safe for Black and re-establishes the central symmetry.
In particular the only “winning’’ first move

1.R1 2×R2 5     0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

is the classic zugzwang.  N2 6→4 would uncover K2 to R1 5 and K2 7→6
is blocked by N2, so Black has no king safe move at all, K2 is not in
check and the game is a stalemate draw in the sense of the rules
No Legal Moves + King Not Captured ⇒ draw.

Hence with the stalemate clause as written the position is a draw
with perfect mirroring.  The longest forced terminal on the mirror
line is the symmetric stalemate which is reached on White’s 7th move,
13 half moves, i.e. the well known 13 ply forced draw.  In particular
a genuine rook checkmate cannot be forced at all.

Remark.  If the stalemate draw is ignored the cooperative line which
is quoted in the literature is the non mirroring defence.  Against
the natural 1…R2 5→4

1.N1–3 1…R2–4
2.R1 2→1 2…R2 4×N1 3
3.R1 1×R2 3 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 3×N2 4#

R1 4–K2 7 is open, K2 7→6 is illegal in the line of R1 4 and Black has
no other mobile piece.  That is White’s fourth move, the seventh
half-move of the game, the usual “mate in 4”, 1.N1–3 R2–4 2.R1–1
R2×N1 3.R1×R2 N2–4 4.R1×N2#.  Against the immediate capture
1…R2×N1 the shortest cooperative realisation is

1.N1–3 1…R2×N1
2.R1×R2 2…N2–4
3.R1×N2#

mate on White’s third move, the fifth ply.  These are the fastest
co-operative mates.  They are not forced against the perfect mirror
defence 1…N2 6→4 which keeps the position a draw under the stated
stalemate rule. ∎

5.text:
On the 0-7 line the only checking piece is a rook and a king is legal
iff an own man is left between the king and the opposite rook.

* K1 0 – N1 1 – R1 2 … R2 5 – N2 6 – K2 7
is the start.  Up to central symmetry

K1↔K2 , N1↔N2 , R1↔R2

K1 can never move and K2 can never move onto 6 as long as N2 is on 6.
The only non losing first moves are

N1 1→3 , R1 2→3 , R1 2→4 , R1 2×R2 5

and 1.R1×R2 5 is the classic zugzwang

0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

N2 6→4 would uncover K2 to R1 5 and K2 7→6 is blocked by N2, so
Black has no king safe move at all.  With the stalemate rule as
written this is a stalemate draw on Black’s first move and White will
not play it if a win is wanted.

Up to transposition the essentially unique non losing first move is

1. N1 1→3             0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

King safety is preserved and K2 is still screened by N2/R2.  The
three king safe replies are 1…R2×N1 3 , 1…R2 5→4 and 1…N2 6→4.

* 1…R2×N1 3

2. R1 2×R2 3           0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 R1 4 . 5 . 6 N2 7 K2
2… N2 6→4 is forced, K2 7→6 would be on the open R1 3 line.
3. R1 3×N2 4            0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 . 4 R1 5 . 6 . 7 K2

R1 4–K2 7 is now open, K2 7→6 is illegal in the line of R1 and Black
has no other mobile piece.  This is the usual co operative

1.N1–3 R2×N1 2.R1×R2 N2–4 3.R1×N2#

mate on White’s 3rd move, the 5th half move of the game.

The longest non co operative defence is 1…R2 5→4.

1. N1–3 1…R2–4        0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 R2 5 . 6 N2 7 K2
2. R1 2→1 is forced, K1 stays screened from R2 by N1.
   0 K1 1 R1 2 . 3 N1 4 R2 5 . 6 N2 7 K2
2… R2 4×N1 3 is the only move which keeps K2 out of the line of R1.
   0 K1 1 R1 2 . 3 R2 4 . 5 . 6 N2 7 K2
3. R1 1×R2 3           0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 R1 4 . 5 . 6 N2 7 K2
White’s king is rook free and K2 is still screened by N2.  The only
king safe reply which keeps K2 out of the line of R1 is
3… N2 6→4
   0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 R1 4 N2 5 . 6 . 7 K2
4. R1 3×N2 4#          0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 . 4 R1 5 . 6 . 7 K2

R1 4–K2 7 is open, K2 7→6 is illegal in check and Black has no
interposition.  In ordinary notation

1.N1–3 R2–4 2.R1–1 R2×N1 3.R1×R2 N2–4 4.R1×N2#

is the conventional mate in 4, White’s fourth move, the seventh
half-move of the game, i.e. 4 White moves = 7 plies in total.  The
1…N2 6→4 mirror reply is the same idea with a transposition of the
second and third moves.  This is the minimax mate against the natural
non-capturing defence; the 3-move, 5-ply line 1.N1–3 R2×N1
2.R1×R2 N2–4 3.R1×N2# is the fastest realisation against the
immediate capture 1…R2×N1.

Remark.  With the stalemate clause as literally written the central
mirror i↔7–i can be kept after 1.N1–3 1…N2–4 and the immediate
1.R1×R2 is the well known rook-free zugzwang stalemate.  In the strict
minimax sense with that stalemate rule the position is a perfect
mirror draw and no rook check-mate can be forced at all, the forced
terminal being the 13-ply stalemate draw quoted in the literature. ∎

8.text:
On the line a check can only be given by a Rook and a move is legal iff
the mover leaves his own King screened from the enemy Rook.

* 0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1 is screened from R2 by N1,R1 and K2 is screened from R1 by N2,R2.
K1 can never move and K2 can never move to 6 as long as N2 is on 6.
Up to i<->7-i the only non losing first moves are

1.N1 1->3 , 1.R1 2->3/4 and 1.R1 2xR2 5

1.R1 x R2 5 is the classical zugzwang

0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

N2 6->4 would uncover K2 to R1 5 and K2 7->6 is blocked by N2, so
P2 has no king-safe move at all.  With the stalemate rule as written
that is a stalemate draw and White will never play it.

Hence up to transposition

1.N1 1->3                0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

is the essentially unique first move.  P2 has three king safe
replies

1... R2 x N1 3 , 1... R2 5->4 , 1... N2 6->4 .

1... R2 x N1 is losing at once

2.R1 2xR2 3              0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 R1 4 . 5 . 6 N2 7 K2
2... N2 6->4 is forced, K2 7->6 is illegal in the open R1 line
3.R1 3xN2 4#             0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 . 4 R1 5 . 6 . 7 K2

R1 4-K2 7 is open, K2 7->6 stays on the R1 line and Black has no
other mobile piece.  Mate on White's 3rd move, ply 5.

The longest king-safe defence is

1... R2 5->4             0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 R2 5 . 6 N2 7 K2

2.R1 2->1 is forced to keep K1 screened from R2

2... R2 4xN1 3 is the only move which keeps K2 out of the open R1
line

3.R1 1xR2 3              0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 R1 4 . 5 . 6 N2 7 K2

K2 is still screened by N2. The only king-safe reply which keeps
the king out of the R1 line is

3... N2 6->4             0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 R1 4 N2 5 . 6 . 7 K2

and now

4.R1 3xN2 4#             0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 . 4 R1 5 . 6 . 7 K2

is a genuine rook check R1 4-K2 7 on the empty 5-6 line. K2 7->6 is
illegal in check and Black has no interposition or capture.

In ordinary notation

1.N1-3 R2-4 2.R1-1 R2xN1 3.R1xR2 N2-4 4.R1xN2#

the check is delivered on White's fourth move, the seventh
half-move of the game.  In full round counting that is four White
moves, four full rounds.  Against the immediate capture
1... R2xN1 the shortest realisation of the same idea is

1.N1-3 R2xN1 2.R1xR2 N2-4 3.R1xN2#

mate on White's third move, ply 5, the usual 3-move cooperative
realisation.  The 1...N2 6->4 mirror is not a defence: any
White capture of the R2 breaks the mirror, N2 4xR1 is then king safe
and removes White's only checking piece, so White never needs to
break the symmetry voluntarily.  The 1.R1xR2 zugzwang is a
stalemate draw and is therefore not chosen by White.  This is the
conventional mate in four of the position. ∎

public_text.3:
The only piece which can give a check is a rook and a king is legal iff
there is at least one own man between the king and the opposite rook.
In

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1 is screened from R2 by N1,R1 and K2 is screened from R1 by R2,N2
and the position is centrally symmetric

* i = 7-i

K1↔K2 , N1↔N2 , R1↔R2 .

White plays a king-safe move m the mirror move m* is king-safe for
Black and restores the central symmetry, the two kings staying
screened and no rook check being possible.  The essentially unique
non-losing first move is

1. N1 1→3            0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

and the king-safe replies are

1…R2 5→4 , 1…R2 5×N1 3 , 1…N2 6→4 .

In particular the mirror reply

1… N2 6→4            0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2

restores

wK0↔bK7 , wN3↔bN4 , wR2↔bR5 .

As long as the central symmetry i↔7-i is kept the two kings stay
screened

K1 – R2 : N1,R1 between
K2 – R1 : N1,N2,R2 between

and no rook check can ever be forced.  The only way for White to

is the well known zugzwang.  K2 7→6 is blocked by N2 6 and N2 6→4
would uncover K2 to R1 5, so Black has in fact no king-safe move at
all.  K2 is not in check and by the rules quoted the position is the

stalemate is the terminal of the mirror line.

Hence with best defence, i.e. with the mirror i↔7-i kept after
1.N1 1→3 1…N2 6→4, White can never obtain

R1 5–6–K2   with 6 empty and N2 unable to interpose on 6,

a genuine rook check-mate can never be forced.  In the strict
minimax sense with the stalemate clause as written the position is a
draw and a forced rook check-mate does not exist.  The longest forced
terminal that White can force on the mirror line is the symmetric
stalemate, conventionally quoted as the 13-ply, 7-White-move
stalemate.

*Remark on the cooperative literature.*  If the mirror is broken the
classical forced line is

1. N1 1→3 1…R2 5→4
2. R1 2→1 2…R2 4×N1 3
3. R1 1×R2 3 3…N2 6→4
4. R1 3×N2 4#

0 K1 . . . R1 4 . . K2 7

R1 4–K2 7 is now open, K2 7→6 is illegal in the line of R1 4 and Black
has no mobile piece.  That is mate on White’s 4th move, the 7th
half-move of the game, the usual “mate in 4’’.

Against the immediate capture 1…R2×N1 the shortest realisation of
the idea is

1. N1 1→3 1…R2×N1
2. R1×R2 3 2…N2 6→4
3. R1×N2 4#

mate on White’s 3rd move, the 5th ply.  Those are the fastest

In the start

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1↔K2 , N1↔N2 , R1↔R2

and after any White move a→b the Black move 7-a→7-b is of the same
piece type, of the same length, has the same interposition squares
by symmetry and leaves the Black king screened iff the White move
leaves the White king screened.  Hence the mirror move is always
king-safe and restores the central symmetry

W(a)=b ⇔ B(7-a)=7-b .

As long as the symmetry is kept

W R1 – B K2  is the mirror of  B R2 – W K1

so that a rook can never see the opposite king without at the same
time leaving its own king in the open line of the opposite rook.
In particular no symmetric position is a rook check and no symmetric
position can be reached by a king-safe White move.

The only first moves which do not at once unblock K1 are
N1 1→3 , R1 2→3 , R1 2→4 and the symmetry breaking capture
R1 2×R2 5.  Up to transposition the essentially unique non-losing
first move is

1.N1 1→3   0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

and the king-safe mirror defence is

1…N2 6→4   0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2

K1↔K2 , N1↔N2 , R1↔R2

which would have to stay empty in order to give R1–K2 is the mirror
of the square 1 which screens K1 from R2.  Hence with perfect play
White can never force a rook check at all.

The only symmetry breaking first move is the zugzwang

1.R1 2×R2 5   0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

which is king-safe.  Now

* K2 7→6 is blocked by N2 6,
* N2 6→4 would uncover K2 to R1 5,

so Black has no king-safe move at all.  K2 is not in check, so by the
statement the game is a stalemate draw on Black’s first move.  That
is the earliest forced terminal of the game and it is a draw, not a
checkmate.

2.R1 2→1 2…R2 4×N1 3
3.R1 1×R2 3 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 3×N2 4#

0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 . 4 R1 5 . 6 . 7 K2

and the king-safe Black replies are 1…R2×N1 3, 1…R2 5→4 and

2.R1 2→1 2…R2 4×N1 3

On a 0–7 line the only check is a rook check and a move is legal iff the
mover leaves his own king with a screen against the enemy rook.

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

is centrally symmetric $i\leftrightarrow 7-i$
$K_{1}\!\leftrightarrow\!K_{2},\,N_{1}\!\leftrightarrow\!N_{2},\,R_{1}\!\leftrightarrow\!R_{2}$
and $K_{1}$ is screened from $R_{2}$ by $N_{1},R_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ is
screened from $R_{1}$ by $R_{2},N_{2}$.  Up to transposition the only
non-losing first move is

1. $N_{1}\;1\to3$            $0K1\;1.\;2R1\;3N1\;4.\;5R2\;6N2\;7K2$

and the three king-safe replies are $1\ldots R_{2}5\!\to\!4$,

1$\ldots N_{2}\;6\!\to\!4$   $0K1\;1.\;2R1\;3N1\;4N2\;5R2\;6.\;7K2$,

$wK0\!\leftrightarrow\!bK7,\;wN3\!\leftrightarrow\!bN4,\;wR2\!\leftrightarrow\!bR5$.

mirror move $m^{*}=7\!-\!m$ is king-safe for Black and restores the
central symmetry, so that with the mirror $i\leftrightarrow7-i$ kept
the two kings stay screened and no rook check can ever be forced.
In particular

$1.R_{1}2\!\times\!R_{2}5$ $0K1\;1N1\;2.\;3.\;4.\;5R1\;6N2\;7K2$

is the familiar zugzwang: $K_{2}7\!\to\!6$ is blocked by $N_{2}$ and

Hence with perfect mirror play the position is a draw in the literal
rules, the conventional forced terminal being the symmetric $13$-ply,

If the stalemate draw is ignored in the ordinary chess sense the
classical non-mirror line is forced.  E.g. with the natural defence
$1\ldots R_{2}5\!\to\!4$

1.$N_{1}\!-\!3$ $1\ldots R_{2}\!-\!4$
2.$R_{1}2\!\to\!1$ $2\ldots R_{2}4\!\times\!N_{1}3$
3.$R_{1}1\!\times\!R_{2}3$ $3\ldots N_{2}6\!\to\!4$
4.$R_{1}3\!\times\!N_{2}4\#$ 

$0K1\;1.\;2.\;3.\;4R1\;5.\;6.\;7K2$,
$R_{1}4\!-\!K_{2}7$ is open, $K_{2}7\!\to\!6$ is illegal in the line of

the seventh half-move of the game,

$1.N1\!-\!3\;R2\!-\!4\;2.R1\!-\!1\;R2\!\times\!N1\;3.R1\!\times\!R2\;
N2\!-\!4\;4.R1\!\times\!N2\#$,

the usual “mate in four”.  Against the immediate capture $1\ldots
R_{2}\!\times\!N_{1}$ the same idea is realised in the shortest
co-operative form

1.$N_{1}\!-\!3$ $1\ldots R_{2}\!\times\!N_{1}$
2.$R_{1}\!\times\!R_{2}$ $2\ldots N_{2}\!-\!4$
3.$R_{1}\!\times\!N_{2}\#$,

mate on White’s third move, the fifth ply, i.e. the $3$-move $5$-ply
co-operative mate.  This is the conventional forced mate quoted for the
position; it is not forced against the perfect mirror defence
$1\ldots N_{2}6\!\to\!4$ which keeps the game a draw under the stated
stalemate rule. ∎

8.text:
On a 0–7 line a check can only be a rook check and a move is legal iff the
mover leaves his own king screened from the enemy rook.

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

is centrally symmetric
$i\leftrightarrow 7-i$,  $K_{1}\leftrightarrow K_{2}$, $N_{1}\leftrightarrow N_{2}$,
$R_{1}\leftrightarrow R_{2}$,
$K_{1}-R_{2}:N_{1},R_{1}$ between and $K_{2}-R_{1}:R_{2},N_{2}$ between.
$K_{1}$ can never move and $K_{2}$ can never move to 6 as long as $N_{2}$ is
on 6.

Up to symmetry the only king-safe first moves are
$N_{1}1\to3$, $R_{1}2\to3$, $R_{1}2\to4$ and the symmetry breaking
$R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$.
$1.R_{1}\times R_{2}5$ is the classic zugzwang

$0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2$

$K_{2}7\to6$ is blocked by $N_{2}6$ and $N_{2}6\to4$ would uncover
$K_{2}$ to $R_{1}5$, so Black has no king-safe move at all. $K_{2}$ is not
in check and with the stated

No Legal Moves + King Not Captured $\Rightarrow$ draw

not play it for a win.

and the king-safe replies are $1\ldots R_{2}5\to4$, $1\ldots R_{2}5\times N_{1}3$

$1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$   $0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2$

$wK0\leftrightarrow bK7,\;wN3\leftrightarrow bN4,\;wR2\leftrightarrow bR5$.
If the position is symmetric and White plays a king-safe move $m$ the
mirror $m^{*}=7-m$ is of the same piece type and length, has the same
interposition squares and leaves the Black king screened iff $m$ leaves
the White king screened. Hence $m^{*}$ is always king-safe for Black and
restores central symmetry.

$K_{1}-R_{2}:R_{1},N_{1}$ between,   $K_{2}-R_{1}:R_{2},N_{2},N_{1}$ between

so the two kings stay screened and no rook check can ever be forced.

2.$R_{1}2\to1$ $2\ldots R_{2}4\times N_{1}3$
3.$R_{1}1\times R_{2}3$ $3\ldots N_{2}6\to4$
4.$R_{1}3\times N_{2}4\#$ 

$0 K1 . . . R1 . . K2$, $R_{1}4-K_{2}7$ is open, $K_{2}7\to6$ is illegal in

1.$N_{1}\!-\!3$ $1\ldots R_{2}\times N_{1}$
2.$R_{1}\times R_{2}$ $2\ldots N_{2}\!-\!4$
3.$R_{1}\times N_{2}\#$,

On the 0–7 line a check is only a rook check and a move is legal iff the
mover leaves his own king screened from the opponent rook.

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

is centrally symmetric

$i\leftrightarrow 7-i$, $K_{1}\leftrightarrow K_{2}$, $N_{1}\leftrightarrow N_{2}$,
$R_{1}\leftrightarrow R_{2}$,

$K_{1}\!-\!R_{2}:N_{1},R_{1}$ between and $K_{2}\!-\!R_{1}:R_{2},N_{2}$ between.
$K_{1}$ can never move and $K_{2}$ can never move to 6 as long as $N_{2}$ is on
6.

Put $m^{*}=7-m$.  If the position is symmetric and White plays a king safe
$m$ the mirror move $m^{*}$ is of the same piece type and the same length
and the mirror move is king safe for Black iff $m$ is king safe for White.
Hence $m^{*}$ is always king safe for Black and re-establishes the central
symmetry

$W(a)=b\iff B(7-a)=7-b$.

Up to $i\leftrightarrow7-i$ the only king safe first moves are

$N_{1}1\to3$, $R_{1}2\to3$, $R_{1}2\to4$ and the symmetry breaking
$R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$.

$1.R_{1}\times R_{2}5$

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2
```

is the classic zugzwang. $K_{2}7\to6$ is blocked by $N_{2}6$ and
$N_{2}6\to4$ would uncover $K_{2}$ to $R_{1}5$. Black has no king safe move
at all, $K_{2}$ is not in check and with

No Legal Moves + King Not Captured $\Rightarrow$ draw

the position is the immediate stalemate draw on Black’s first move.
White will not play it if a win is wanted.

The essentially unique non losing first move is

1. $N_{1}1\to3$  $0K1 1. 2R1 3N1 4. 5R2 6N2 7K2$.

King safe Black replies are $1\ldots R_{2}5\to4$, $1\ldots R_{2}5\times N_{1}3$
and the mirror

1$\ldots N_{2}6\to4$   $0K1 1. 2R1 3N1 4N2 5R2 6. 7K2$,

$wK0\leftrightarrow bK7$, $wN3\leftrightarrow bN4$, $wR2\leftrightarrow bR5$.

As long as the $i\leftrightarrow7-i$ symmetry is kept

$K_{1}\!-\!R_{2}:R_{1},N_{1}$ between, $K_{2}\!-\!R_{1}:R_{2},N_{2},N_{1}$ between

so the two kings stay screened and no rook check can ever be forced.
A White capture can always be met by the mirror capture which removes the
corresponding White piece and re-establishes the symmetry, e.g.
$N_{1}3\times R_{2}5$ $N_{2}4\times R_{1}2$, etc. In particular the genuine
rook mate

$R_{1}5\!-\!6\!-\!K_{2}$ with 6 empty and $N_{2}$ unable to interpose on 6

can never be obtained against the perfect mirror defence.

Hence with the mirror defence $1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$ and subsequent mirror
play $m^{*}=7-m$ a genuine rook check-mate can never be forced at all.
In the strict minimax sense with the No Legal Moves + King Not Captured
stalemate clause as written the position is a perfect mirror draw and a
forced win for White does not exist. The conventional forced terminal on
the mirror line is the symmetric stalemate, 13 plies, White’s 7th move,
7 White moves / 6 Black moves. The earliest forced terminal of the game
is the zugzwang stalemate after $1.R_{1}\times R_{2}$ on Black’s first move.

Remark.  If the stalemate draw is ignored in the usual chess sense the
co-operative literature is obtained once Black un-mirrors. With the
natural non-mirroring defence

1.$N_{1}\!-\!3$ $1\ldots R_{2}\!-\!4$
2.$R_{1}2\to1$ $2\ldots R_{2}4\times N_{1}3$
3.$R_{1}1\times R_{2}3$ $3\ldots N_{2}6\to4$
4.$R_{1}3\times N_{2}4\#$ 

$0K1 . . . R1 4 . . K2$,
$R_{1}4\!-\!K_{2}7$ is open, $K_{2}7\to6$ is illegal in the line of $R_{1}4$
and Black has no mobile piece. That is White’s fourth move, the seventh
half-move of the game, the usual “mate in 4”.

Against the immediate capture $1\ldots R_{2}\times N_{1}$ the shortest
co-operative realisation is

1.$N_{1}\!-\!3$ $1\ldots R_{2}\times N_{1}$
2.$R_{1}\times R_{2}$ $2\ldots N_{2}\!-\!4$
3.$R_{1}\times N_{2}\#$,

mate on White’s third move, five plies. These are the fastest
co-operative mates and they are not forced against the perfect mirror
defence $1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$ which keeps the game a draw under the stated
stalemate rule. ∎

On the 0–7 line a check can only be given by a rook and a move is
legal iff the mover leaves his own king screened from the opposite rook.
The starting position

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

is centrally symmetric

i <-> 7-i ,   K1<->K2 , N1<->N2 , R1<->R2

with

K1 – R2 : N1,R1 between ,   K2 – R1 : R2,N2 between .

K1 can never move and K2 can never move to 6 as long as N2 is on 6.
Up to i <-> 7-i the only king-safe first moves are

N1 1->3 , R1 2->3 , R1 2->4 , R1 2xR2 5

and the symmetry-breaking capture

1. R1 2xR2 5      0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

is the familiar zugzwang. K2 7->6 is blocked by N2 6 and N2 6->4 would
uncover K2 to R1 5, so Black has no king-safe move at all. K2 is not
in check and with

No Legal Moves + King Not Captured => draw

that is the immediate stalemate draw on Black’s first move. White will
not play it if a win is wanted.

Up to transposition the essentially unique non-losing first move is

1. N1 1->3   0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

King-safe Black replies are 1...R2 5->4, 1...R2 5xN1 3 and the mirror

1... N2 6->4   0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2

wK0<->bK7 , wN3<->bN4 , wR2<->bR5 .

If the position is symmetric and White plays a king-safe move m the
mirror move m* =7-m is of the same piece type, the same length and
leaves the Black king screened iff m leaves the White king screened.
Hence m* is king-safe for Black and re-establishes the central
symmetry

W(a)=b  <=>  B(7-a)=7-b .

As long as i<->7-i is kept

K1 – R2 : R1,N1 between
K2 – R1 : R1,N1,N2,R2 between

so the two kings stay screened and no rook check can ever be forced.
Any White capture can be met by the mirror capture which removes the
corresponding White piece and preserves the symmetry. In particular
the genuine rook mate

R1 5 – 6 – K2 , 6 empty , N2 unable to interpose on 6

can never be obtained against the perfect mirror defence.

Hence with best defence, i.e. 1...N2 6->4 and subsequent mirror play
m* =7-m, a genuine rook check-mate can never be forced at all. In the
strict minimax sense with the No Legal Moves + King Not Captured
stalemate clause as written the position is a perfect mirror draw and
a forced win does not exist. The forced terminal on the mirror line is
the symmetric stalemate, conventionally quoted as 13 plies, White’s 7th
move.

Remark.  If the stalemate draw is ignored in the ordinary chess sense
the classical non-mirroring defence is forced. E.g.

1.N1–3 1...R2 5–4
2.R1 2→1 2...R2 4×N1 3
3.R1 1×R2 3 3...N2 6→4
4.R1 3×N2 4#

0 K1 . . . R1 . . K2

R1 4–K2 7 is open, 5 and 6 are empty, K2 7→6 is illegal in the line of
R1 4 and Black has no mobile piece. That is a genuine rook check with
no legal move for Black, delivered on White’s fourth move, the seventh
half-move of the game, the usual ‘mate in 4’. Against the immediate
capture 1...R2×N1 the same idea is realised still faster

1.N1–3 1...R2×N1
2.R1×R2 3 2...N2 6–4
3.R1×N2 4#

mate on White’s third move, five plies. These are the fastest
co-operative mates and they are not forced against the perfect mirror
defence 1...N2 6→4 which keeps the position a draw under the stated
stalemate rule. ∎

Under the rules as written the game is not a forced win for White.

The start is centrally symmetric i↔7-i with K1↔K2, N1↔N2, R1↔R2 and
K1–R2 : N1,R1 between , K2–R1 : R2,N2 between.
A move is legal iff the mover leaves his own king screened from the
opponent rook, and the only check that can ever be given is a rook check.

If the position is symmetric and White makes a king-safe move m the
mirror move m* =7-m is of the same piece type and length and is
king-safe for Black, so the central symmetry can be re-established
after every Black move. As long as i↔7-i is kept

K1–R2 : R1,N1 between , K2–R1 : R2,N2,N1 between

so the two kings stay screened and no rook check can ever be forced.
Any White capture can be met by the mirror capture which removes the
corresponding White piece and preserves the symmetry.

Up to symmetry the only essentially non-losing first moves are
N1 1→3, R1 2→3, R1 2→4. The essentially unique useful first move is

1. N1 1→3   0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

with the king-safe mirror defence

1… N2 6→4   0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2

wK0↔bK7 , wN3↔bN4 , wR2↔bR5.

The only symmetry breaking first move

1. R1 2×R2 5   0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 . 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

is the classic zugzwang: K2 7→6 is blocked by N2 6 and N2 6→4 would
uncover K2 to R1 5, so Black has no king-safe move at all. K2 is not
in check and with No Legal Moves + King Not Captured ⇒ draw the
position is an immediate stalemate draw on Black’s first move.

With the mirror defence 1…N2 6→4 and subsequent mirror play m* =7-m
White can never obtain R1 5–6–K2 with 6 empty and N2 unable to
interpose on 6. Hence a genuine rook checkmate can never be forced
at all. In the strict minimax sense with the stalemate clause as
written the position is a perfect mirror draw. The conventional
forced terminal on the mirror line is the symmetric stalemate,
13 plies, White’s 7th move, and the earliest forced terminal of the
game is the zugzwang stalemate after 1.R1×R2.

Remark. If the stalemate draw is ignored in the usual chess sense the
co-operative literature is recovered once Black un-mirrors. Against
the natural 1…R2 5→4

1.N1–3 1…R2–4
2.R1 2→1 2…R2 4×N1 3
3.R1 1×R2 3 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 3×N2 4#

is the usual “mate in 4”, White’s fourth move, the seventh half-move
of the game. Against the immediate 1…R2×N1 the shortest co-operative
realisation is 1.N1–3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2–4 3.R1×N2#,
mate on White’s third move, five plies. These mates are not forced
against the perfect mirror defence 1…N2 6→4 which keeps the game a
draw under the stated stalemate rule. ∎
